transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-07-14
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Michael Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Redwood CSM), Daniel Ortiz (CTO, Argonaut), Sara Bloom (ML Engineer), Kevin Ma (Infra), Jordan Lee (Product)

Auto-generated Summary:
Argonaut is evaluating an exit from OpenAI for cost predictability and better routing to lower-cost model variants. They want to understand Redwood hosted vs dedicated vs private (VPC/on-prem), quantization impacts, and runtime compatibility with their existing vLLM/TGI tooling. Primary concerns: latency p95, prompt/response parity, KMS/encryption, and an enterprise-friendly pilot path.

Topics:
- Model parity and eval setup
- Streaming and function-calling fidelity
- Quantization and unit-cost tradeoffs
- VPC/private deployment constraints and KMS/HSM
- Rollout and fallback routing strategies
- Security and compliance (SOC2, audit logs, SSO)

Action items (brief): see metadata action_items above

Transcript body:
[00:00] Michael Chen: Okay, hi everyone, this is Michael from Redwood. Thanks for carving out the time. Do you want to quick intros?
[00:12] Daniel Ortiz: Yeah, I'm Daniel, CTO at Argonaut, uh, we've got Sara our ML engineer, Kevin on infra and Jordan from product. We're trying to figure out an exit strategy from OpenAI and what the host/dedicated/private options look like.
[00:25] Michael Chen: Great. Quick level set from our side, Priya's our SE who'll cover performance and parity, Lena's on CS and will own pilot logistics.
[00:32] Priya Kapoor: Hi all. Happy to dig into the vLLM/TGI compatibility questions — we've done several migrations where customers keep their eval harness and we map it to Redwood's hosted and dedicated runtimes.
[00:44] Jordan Lee: Cool. For context, our main product is a conversational assistant embedded in our web app. We've been on OpenAI for about a year; cost has spiked, and we need more predictable unit economics and fallback policies.
[00:56] Sara Bloom: Also we use vLLM internally for local experiments and TGI for some model conversions; want to know if that pipeline will still work.
[01:05] Priya Kapoor: Totally. Two high level paths: 1) Redwood Hosted — fastest time to value, we manage runtime and you call our API; 2) Redwood Dedicated — reserved capacity in our infra, predictable throughput; 3) Redwood Private — VPC or on-prem, customer managed network and KMS. Each has different trade-offs on latency SLO and control.
[01:30] Kevin Ma: On the private option, we need KMS integration — our security folks will insist on HSM-backed key material. Does Redwood support HSM/KMS integrations?
[01:40] Michael Chen: Yes we integrate with customer KMS providers (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and HSMs) in Private and we have options for key isolation in Dedicated. We'll share the integration guide after the call.
[01:50] Daniel Ortiz: And SOC 2? We need evidence for procurement.
[01:54] Lena Ortiz: We are SOC 2 Type II, we can push the pack — I'll send the certs and the security pack today.
[02:01] Sara Bloom: On parity — our main worry is subtle changes in tokenization and streaming formatting. OpenAI streaming includes chunked deltas; will Redwood's streaming match that so our front end doesn't need changes?
[02:15] Priya Kapoor: We support streaming with partial deltas and can mirror common OpenAI patterns, but there are some edge cases where we stream slightly different chunk boundaries. Usually the front end can be unchanged; if you have strict parsing we can run a quick compatibility harness.
[02:30] Jordan Lee: Good. Also, function calling — we use it for structured responses. Any gotchas?
[02:36] Priya Kapoor: We support function-style structured outputs; we can reproduce calling semantics but you'll want to validate complex nested schemas in the parity bench.
[02:45] Michael Chen: Maybe worth calling out the model catalog — we provide open-model variants and Redwood-verified performance profiles. If parity is critical, we can map you to a verified variant and run example prompts.
[02:59] Sara Bloom: We care about quantization too. We run some Llama-family hybrids; what's your position on 8-bit/4-bit quantization and impact on output?
[03:09] Priya Kapoor: Common approach: 8-bit quantization generally preserves parity for many tasks with a small drop in quality that you can usually detect in edge-case completions; 4-bit can be more aggressive but the cost wins are much larger. For customers with strict quality requirements we run comparative evals at multiple quant levels.
[03:26] Daniel Ortiz: Can you quantify cost delta? Like, how much cheaper is a 4-bit path vs hosted OpenAI?
[03:32] Michael Chen: It depends on throughput, but rough order — 4-bit on dedicated or private can be 3–6x cheaper per token when compared to hosted managed OpenAI costs, especially at scale. We'll put more precise numbers in the pilot pricing SOW.
[03:47] Kevin Ma: Our infra team is very strict on latency — p95 has to be under 250ms for short-turn interactions. Can Redwood meet that on hosted?
[03:57] Priya Kapoor: For short requests (<=128 tokens) hosted p95 is region-dependent; in our primary regions we often see ~120–220ms p95 for optimized small-medium open models. Dedicated with reserved capacity can tighten that further and private on-prem can meet sub-100ms depending on hardware.
[04:18] Sara Bloom: When you say optimized kernels and compilers — do you have something like custom CUDA kernels or do you rely on Triton / cuBLAS?
[04:25] Priya Kapoor: We use a mix: optimized kernels, attention optimizations and a kernel selector at runtime — some users call it our compilation layer. For certain model families we ship specialized kernels and fallback options. That is also why vLLM/TGI behavior can differ slightly — they choose different kernels and batching strategies.
[04:44] Daniel Ortiz: We use continuous batching in vLLM; is Redwood's serving runtime continuous-batching friendly?
[04:50] Priya Kapoor: Yes, our runtime supports continuous batching and KV cache management to reduce per-token work. We can tune batch windows to balance latency and throughput.
[05:02] Jordan Lee: About migrations — what's the typical pilot? Do we port a subset of prompts and run A/B?
[05:08] Michael Chen: Typical pilot is 4–6 weeks: baseline data exchange, parity benchmarks on your prompt set, performance benchmarks (latency/cost), and then a canary with traffic split and fallbacks. We'll propose a SOW.
[05:21] Sara Bloom: For parity bench we need identical tokenization. OpenAI sometimes returns different token counts for the same prompt across minor engine versions — how do you account for that?
[05:33] Priya Kapoor: We instrument tokenization in our bench harness and surface token diffs. If tokenization discrepancy is due to model tokenizer differences we can recommend model variants or pre-tokenize on your side and send raw tokens for strict parity.
[05:47] Kevin Ma: If we go Dedicated, how is burst capacity handled? We have occasional spikes from events.
[05:54] Michael Chen: Dedicated includes configurable autoscaling policies and optional burst capacity. You can set hard capacity and add burst policies that draw from a shared pool for short durations.
[06:02] Daniel Ortiz: What about routing rules — ideally we want cheaper model variants for non-critical queries and a high-quality model for important flows. Can we route by route, by endpoint, or per-request?
[06:13] Priya Kapoor: Yes, smart routing is a core feature. You can route by policy (latency SLO, cost tier, region, or customer tier) and set automatic fallbacks if a variant fails. Many customers implement a primary high-quality model and a cheaper fallback for low-risk requests.
[06:27] Jordan Lee: Are there SDKs for in-app switching?
[06:30] Michael Chen: We have SDKs and header-based routing where you can pass metadata to influence model selection.
[06:37] Sara Bloom: Two practical questions — 1) will our current TGI-based conversion artifacts load on Redwood dedicated/private? 2) any code changes for the runtime?
[06:47] Priya Kapoor: Generally yes for artifacts that conform to standard model formats (e.g., Hugging Face). For TGI-specific optimizations we might need small adaptors. We'll run a compatibility test. No major code rewrite is typically needed.
[06:58] Daniel Ortiz: We also do embeddings for semantic search — how does your embedding pricing and vector store guidance look?
[07:06] Michael Chen: We support embeddings via the same API, per-embedding unit pricing. We can run guidance for best-performing models and recommend quantization for offline indexes versus online inference.
[07:17] Kevin Ma: Does Redwood provide audit logs for request/response metadata for compliance?
[07:22] Lena Ortiz: Yes, we have token-level cost breakdowns, per-route logs, and audit trails. For Private deployments you can ship logs to customer-managed sinks or leverage our retention options.
[07:34] Jordan Lee: Our procurement will ask about contractual SLAs — any standard SLA tiers for Dedicated?
[07:39] Michael Chen: Dedicated plans can come with SLA-backed uptime/latency tiers — details will be in the pilot SOW.
[07:47] Sara Bloom: On the parity bench — how do you handle nondeterminism in model outputs so we can compare apples to apples?
[07:55] Priya Kapoor: We run multiple seeds, temperature controls, and n-best comparisons. For strict deterministic checks we can run zero-temperature or use forced-decoding where possible. For creative flows we focus on behavioral/regression metrics like intent accuracy or hallucination rates.
[08:14] Daniel Ortiz: Any examples of customers who left OpenAI and kept function-calling fidelity?
[08:20] Michael Chen: Yes, we've had a few customers who migrated — we can anonymize case notes, but generally it's been feasible with a short remediation cycle to align function schemas and streaming semantics.
[08:34] Kevin Ma: Can you run a quick throat-clearing on pricing structure for pilots? I know we'll get details later but top-level is useful.
[08:41] Michael Chen: High-level: Hosted is usage-based with per-token rates and optional committed discounts. Dedicated is a reserved capacity monthly commit plus variable usage. Private usually has platform licensing plus support and ops. We'll put specific numbers in the SOW tailored to your traffic profile.
[08:59] Jordan Lee: Okay, digging into evils — we have some custom prompt engineering that relies on OpenAI-specific stop-token behavior. Does Redwood emulate stop sequences similarly?
[09:09] Priya Kapoor: We have configurable stop sequence handling and provide options that mimic OpenAI's behavior; we'll validate in the parity harness.
[09:19] Sara Bloom: On the technical deep-dive side, can we schedule a session where you bring in someone who worked on kernel selection and quantization? Could be useful for our ML folks.
[09:28] Priya Kapoor: Absolutely — we can schedule a deep-dive and bring runtime engineers.
[09:33] Daniel Ortiz: About on-prem — our security team will probably ask for an air-gapped deployment option later. Is that offered?
[09:41] Michael Chen: We offer an on-prem package for regulated/air-gapped environments. There is a heavier integration and validation window, but it's supported.
[09:49] Kevin Ma: For private deployments do you support customer VPC peering or do you require a managed VPN?
[09:56] Priya Kapoor: We support VPC peering, private connectivity, and customer-managed VPNs depending on the deployment model.
[10:03] Jordan Lee: Any constraints on the model size/hardware you recommend for the private path?
[10:08] Priya Kapoor: Depends on your models and SLOs: 13B-class models often hit sweet spots for latency/cost; >70B models need more careful hardware planning. We'll give recommendations after seeing your prompts and sequences.
[10:22] Sara Bloom: We have a question — will Redwood allow us to bring our own pretrained weights that might have licensing constraints?
[10:29] Michael Chen: Yes, customers can bring their own models subject to licensing and compliance. We have onboarding checks for license compatibility.
[10:37] Daniel Ortiz: Ok — let's talk risks. Biggest showstoppers for us are parity regressions and encryption/key controls. If you can sign off on those in the pilot, procurement will move fast.
[10:49] Michael Chen: Understood — we'll prioritize parity and KMS/HSM integration in the SOW and bench.
[10:55] Jordan Lee: One more practical — do you support gradual rollouts (canary, A/B)?
[10:59] Priya Kapoor: Yes, rollouts and automatic fallback policies are first-class — you can set per-route canaries, percentage traffic splits, and automatic rollback on error or quality regressions.
[11:12] Lena Ortiz: For the next couple of steps, we'll: 1) send security pack + SOC2, 2) Michael will draft SOW and pilot pricing, 3) Priya will run parity bench once you share prompts.
[11:24] Daniel Ortiz: Sounds good. We'll share a sample corpus and p95 targets — Kevin will drop in the infra slack.
[11:31] Michael Chen: Great, thanks everyone. Any last questions?
[11:36] Sara Bloom: A tiny thing — does Redwood's telemetry reveal prompt text to support error analysis? We need to control PII.
[11:44] Lena Ortiz: You can configure PII redaction and retention — defaults avoid storing raw prompt text unless explicitly enabled for debugging. We'll include details in the security pack.
[11:57] Jordan Lee: Perfect. Thanks all.
[12:00] Michael Chen: Thanks, we'll follow up with the materials.
[12:04] Meeting end.
